title: The ancient churches of the east
hookLine: Copts, Ethiopians, Armenians and Syriacs keep some of the oldest Christian traditions on earth

cards: In the highlands of northern Ethiopia there's a town called Lalibela, where, many centuries ago, whole churches were carved down into the solid red rock. Not built.
Carved, from the top down, like sculptures you can walk into.

On a feast day before dawn, crowds in white shawls fill the trenches around them, and priests chant in Ge'ez, a language no longer spoken in daily life, kept alive in prayer. Drums. Sistrums, little metal rattles.
Swaying. Christianity is often pictured in a European cathedral or an American strip-mall church. Lalibela is a reminder that very old Christian traditions are African and Asian.

teach.b: The Oriental Orthodox churches are a family of six: the Coptic church of Egypt, the Ethiopian and Eritrean churches, the Armenian Apostolic church, the Syriac Orthodox church, and the Malankara church in India.
Oriental just means eastern. Orthodox, yes, but a separate family from the Greek and Russian Orthodox you may know. Why?
Remember Chalcedon, in 451: Christ in two natures. These churches didn't accept that wording.
They held to an older phrase from Cyril of Alexandria: one nature of God the Word made flesh, divine and human united, never mixed and never divided.
Others called them monophysites, one-nature people, a label they reject.
They say miaphysite: one united nature. For centuries each side thought the other had lost something essential.

Then, in the late twentieth century, theologians from these churches, the Eastern Orthodox and the Catholic Church agreed in joint statements that much of the split had been about words, and that they share far more than they thought.
Armenian tradition remembers its king as the first to make Christianity a kingdom's official faith, in the early 300s.
The Ethiopian church loves the story in Acts 8 of an Ethiopian official baptized on a desert road, and a line from the Psalms: "Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God."
Coptic, their old church language, descends from the language of the pharaohs. Syriac is a form of Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke.
These churches have lived through empires, massacres and exile, and some of their people have had to flee their homes.

teach.h: ETHIOPIA SHALL SOON STRETCH OUT HER HANDS UNTO GOD.
teach.b: And every Sunday, they still sing.

how: Oriental Orthodox Christians worship in ancient liturgical languages such as Coptic, Ge'ez, Armenian and Syriac, keep long fasts through the year, and many stand through services that last several hours.

games.q: it's after 451. the council of Chalcedon has said Christ is in two natures. you're a bishop in Egypt who loves Cyril's phrase, one nature of the Word made flesh. what do you do?
o: keep the older phrase, even if it means a split.
games.why: the churches of Egypt, Syria, Armenia and Ethiopia kept their older wording. centuries later, theologians agreed they'd meant much the same thing.

practice: Hold one fact: in Ethiopian Orthodox practice, a church is consecrated with a tabot, a carved tablet standing for the ark of the covenant, kept wrapped in cloth.

Picture the white shawls before dawn, people keeping one way of praying for many centuries. If you pray, pray for these churches and their people far from home; if not, hold them in mind with respect.

wordCard.voice: Oriental Orthodox. The six ancient churches of Egypt, Ethiopia, Eritrea, Armenia, Syria and India, who kept their own way after Chalcedon.

orig.note: Ge'ez: made one, united. The Ethiopian church's own name, Tewahedo, for Christ's one united nature.

carryVoice: Your line: very old, still singing. Ancient, and still here. That's day two hundred eighty-four.
